q-320695.name: Question 1
q-320695.worked_solution:
To factor a sum of squares, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${i}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+49 & ={x}^{2}-(-49) \\  & ={x}^{2}-(49{i}^{2}) \\  & ={x}^{2}-(7i)^{2} \\  & =(x+7i)(x-7i)\end{aligned}
$$

q-46505.name: Question 5
q-46505.worked_solution:
First, let's factor $-1$ from the expression. We have

$$
-4{z}^{2}-81=-(4{z}^{2}+81).
$$

Let's now focus on factoring the expression $(4{z}^{2}+81).$

To factor a sum of squares, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{z}^{2}+81 & =4{z}^{2}-(-81) \\  & =4{z}^{2}-(81{\text{i}}^{2}) \\  & =(2z)^{2}-(9\text{i})^{2} \\  & =(2z+9\text{i})(2z-9\text{i})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our main expression, we get

$$
-(4{z}^{2}+81)=-(2z+9\text{i})(2z-9\text{i}).
$$

q-46534.name: Question 6
q-46534.worked_solution:
First, let's factor $5$ from the expression. We have

$$
45{m}^{2}+5=5(9{m}^{2}+1).
$$

Let's now focus on factoring the expression $(9{m}^{2}+1).$

To factor a sum of squares, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}9{m}^{2}+1 & =9{m}^{2}-(-1) \\  & =(3m)^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2} \\  & =(3m+\text{i})(3m-\text{i})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our main expression, we get

$$
5(9{m}^{2}+1)=5(3m+\text{i})(3m-\text{i}).
$$

a
5(3m+i)(3m−i)
b
15(m+i)(m−i)

(3m+i)(3m−i)
d
(3m+1)(3m−1)

5(3m+1)(3m−1)

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's factor 5 from the expression. We have

45m2+5=5(9m2+1).

Let's now focus on factoring the expression (9m2+1).

To factor a sum of squares, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using i2=−1. Finally, we factor as a difference of squares.

9m2+1=9m2−(−1)=(3m)2−i2=(3m+i)(3m−i)

Finally, substituting this back into our main expression, we get

5(9m2+1)=5(3m+i)(3m−i).

q-371812.worked_solution:
First, let's factor the expression as a perfect square trinomial in ${y}^{2}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}256{y}^{4}+32{y}^{2}+1 & ={(16{y}^{2})}^{2}+2\cdot (16{y}^{2})\cdot 1+{1}^{2} \\  & ={(16{y}^{2}+1)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to factor the sum of squares in the parentheses. To do this, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${i}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}16{y}^{2}+1 & =16{y}^{2}-(-1) \\  & =16{y}^{2}-({i}^{2}) \\  & ={(4y)}^{2}-{(i)}^{2} \\  & =(4y+i)(4y-i)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our main expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}256{y}^{4}+32{y}^{2}+1 & ={(16{y}^{2}+1)}^{2} \\  & ={((4y+i)(4y-i))}^{2} \\  & ={(4y+i)}^{2}{(4y-i)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-87334.name: Question 8
q-87334.worked_solution:
First, let's factor the expression as a perfect square trinomial in ${y}^{2}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}81{y}^{4}+36{y}^{2}+4 & ={(9{y}^{2})}^{2}+2\cdot \,(9{y}^{2})\cdot 2+{2}^{2} \\  & ={(9{y}^{2}+2)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to factor the sum of squares in the parentheses. To do this, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}9{y}^{2}+2 & =9{y}^{2}-(-2) \\  & =9{y}^{2}-(2{\text{i}}^{2}) \\  & =(3y)^{2}-{(\sqrt{2}\,\text{i})}^{2} \\  & =(3y+\sqrt{2}\,\text{i})(3y-\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our main expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}81{y}^{4}+36{y}^{2}+4 & ={(9{y}^{2}+2)}^{2} \\  & =((3y+\sqrt{2}\,\text{i})(3y-\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}))^{2} \\  & =(3y+\sqrt{2}\,\text{i})^{2}(3y-\sqrt{2}\,\text{i})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's factor the expression as a perfect square trinomial in ${w}^{2}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{4}+36{w}^{2}+81 & ={(2{w}^{2})}^{2}+2\cdot (2{w}^{2})\cdot 9+{9}^{2} \\  & =(2{w}^{2}+9)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to factor the sum of squares in the parentheses. To do this, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{w}^{2}+9 & =2{w}^{2}-(-9) \\  & =2{w}^{2}-(9{\text{i}}^{2}) \\  & =(\sqrt{2}w)^{2}-(3\text{i})^{2} \\  & =(\sqrt{2}w+3\text{i})(\sqrt{2}w-3\text{i})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our main expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{4}+36{w}^{2}+81 & =(2{w}^{2}+9)^{2} \\  & =((\sqrt{2}w+3\text{i})(\sqrt{2}w-3\text{i}))^{2} \\  & =(\sqrt{2}w+3\text{i})^{2}(\sqrt{2}w-3\text{i})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
